statement: Data is always a good approximation of reality.
label: False
explanations: Data can never perfectly capture reality.

statement: With training, it is possible to eliminate confirmation bias.
label: False
explanations: Human beings will always be subject to confirmation bias.

statement: As soon as your analysis provides an answer to your domain question, you have conclusively answered the question.
label: False
explanations: The results of your analysis correspond to just one possible answer that you could have obtained. Rather than proof of your conclusion, your analysis provides evidence of your conclusion.

statement: Results computed from a dataset that is collected today may not apply to data that will be collected in the future, even if both datasets are collected using the same mechanism.
label: True
explanations: Even if the data is collected using the same mechanism, the underlying real-world trends may have changed.

statement: There are multiple ways to demonstrate the predictability of your results.
label: True
explanations: There are many ways that you can evaluate the predictability of your results, including showing that they are in line with domain knowledge and that they reemerge in future data.

statement: PCS evaluations are necessary only when you will be presenting your results to an external audience.
label: False
explanations: It is also important for the analyst themselves to determine whether their results are predictable and stable, even if they will not be presenting them to an external audience.

statement: There is only one correct way to conduct every data analysis.
label: False
explanations: There is no single correct way that an analysis should be conducted; indeed there are often many (that's not to say that there are no incorrect ways).

statement: Every data science project must progress through every stage of the DSLC.
label: False
explanations: While some of the stages are very important in every project, such as the data cleaning and the exploratory data analysis (EDA) stages, there are some stages, such as the prediction stage, that may not be relevant to all projects.

statement: PCS uncertainty quantification is unrelated to traditional statistical inference.
label: False
explanations: PCS uncertainty quantification is an extension of traditional statistical inference that takes into consideration uncertainty arising from judgment calls, rather than just from the data sampling mechanism (as in traditional statistical inference).

statement: Communication with domain experts is only important during the problem formulation stage.
label: False
explanations: Communication with domain experts is important throughout the entire DSLC.

statement: There are many ways to formulate a data science problem.
label: True
explanations: Every data science problem can be formulated in multiple different ways.

statement: Once you have moved on to a new stage of the DSLC, it is OK to return to and update previous stages.
label: True
explanations: The DSLC is non-linear. Often you will learn things about your data in the later stages that will require you to backtrack to your cleaning or preprocessing steps or conduct further exploration.

statement: The judgment calls that you make during data cleaning can have an impact on your downstream results.
label: True
explanations: It is very common for results to be affected by the judgment calls made early in the DSLC, including at the data cleaning stage.

statement: PCS evaluations can help prevent data snooping.
label: True
explanations: Since PCS evaluations involve conducting stress tests of your results in new scenarios (such as using future data), it can help identify when a finding was just a reflection of the coincidental patterns that exist among specific data points used to generate them, which is another way of saying that it can help prevent data snooping.

statement: It is OK to modify your original raw data file if you document the edits that you made.
label: False
explanations: While it is OK to edit a copy of your original raw data file if you absolutely must make manual edits (and be sure to document any edits that you make), you should avoid editing the original file itself.

statement: It is bad practice to rerun the code that cleans your data.
label: False
explanations: Quite the opposite: you should regularly rerun all your code, including the code that cleans your data, to maximize the reproducibility potential of your results.

statement: R is better than Python for data science.
label: False
explanations: This is subjective, but we strongly believe that neither language is universally better than the other for data science (although each language may be better than the other for some particular types of projects).

statement: The term "reproducibility" is defined as being able to reproduce the same results on alternative data.
label: False
explanations: There is a broad spectrum of types of reproducibility, and this definition encompasses just one of them.

statement: The "reproducibility crisis" is a problem unique to data science, and is not an issue in traditional scientific fields.
label: False
explanations: The reproducibility crisis is a problem that is affecting a range of scientific fields.

statement: If someone else cannot reproduce your results (based on any definition of reproducibility), then your results must be wrong.
label: False
explanations: It is possible that the other person is not correctly implementing their reproduction or that they simply arrived at a different answer due to different humans making different judgment calls.

statement: If someone else manages to reproduce your results (using their own independent data and by conducting their own analyses), then this proves that your results are correct.
label: False
explanations: This is strong evidence that your results are "trustworthy," but this doesn't prove that your results are "correct." Moreover, you may both be wrong!

statement: Your dslc_documentation files can contain code.
label: True
explanations: Your dslc_documentation files can (and should) contain code.

statement: A good technique for increasing the reproducibility of your results (in the context of ensuring that you get the same results every time you run it) is to rerun your code from scratch often.
label: True
explanations: This is an excellent way to increase the chance that your results are reproducible, at least in the context of ensuring that you get the same results every time that your code is run.

statement: Data cleaning is an optional part of the DSLC.
label: False
explanations: Every dataset should at least be examined to determine if it needs to be cleaned.

statement: The best way to handle missing values is to remove the rows with missing values.
label: False
explanations: Removing the offending rows is one way to handle missing values, but it is rarely the best way since it is likely to introduce bias into your data. Often, it is better to impute missing values or remove unimportant columns with large numbers of missing values.

statement: An unusual or surprising value should be treated as invalid.
label: False
explanations: Just because a value is surprising doesn't mean that it is incorrect or invalid. It does, however, warrant further exploration (e.g., by asking the person who collected the data how such a value might have arisen). If it is clear that the value is invalid or incorrect, then you may want to replace it with a missing value, but this should not be automatic.

statement: There is a single correct way to clean every dataset.
label: False
explanations: There are many reasonable ways to clean every dataset, and everyone will likely clean the same dataset slightly differently.

statement: You should avoid exploring your data before you clean it.
label: False
explanations: Exploring your data is part of cleaning it.

statement: You must write separate cleaning and preprocessing functions.
label: False
explanations: While we often find it helpful to keep the cleaning and preprocessing stages separate (so we can explore a clean version of the data that has not been modified to suit a particular algorithm), it is not necessary to do so if it feels overly complicated.

statement: A different preprocessing function is needed for each algorithm that you apply.
label: False
explanations: You can instead add different arguments to your preprocessing function to create different versions of your data for algorithms with different formatting requirements.

statement: You should avoid modifying the original data file itself; instead, you should try to modify it only within your programming environment.
label: True
explanations: This minimizes the chance that you will accidentally corrupt the original data file.

statement: A clean dataset can contain missing values.
label: True
explanations: Clean data can contain missing values if they are properly formatted as missing (e.g., as NA values in R).

statement: A preprocessed dataset can contain missing values.
label: True
explanations: Since the preprocessing steps that you will implement depend on the algorithm/analysis that you will conduct, missing values may or may not be a problem. In most (but not all) scenarios, however, you will end up removing or imputing missing values during preprocessing.

statement: The set of valid values for a variable is usually determined based on domain knowledge and how the data was collected.
label: True
explanations: The set of valid values for a variable is indeed usually determined based on domain knowledge and how the data was collected.

statement: It is generally recommended that you split your data into training, validation, and test sets before cleaning it.
label: True
explanations: This is because we don't want to use information from the validation and test sets when cleaning your training data.

statement: It is a good idea to add color to a plot, even when the color does not convey information.
label: False
explanations: We recommend using color sparingly, and only if it adds information. Color can be added for purely aesthetic purposes, but its use should be kept as simple as possible.

statement: The correlation between two numeric variables describes the angle of the linear relationship in a scatterplot.
label: False
explanations: The correlation describes the tightness of the points around a line that can be at any angle.

statement: The mean is a better summary of a typical value than the median when there are outliers present.
label: False
explanations: Whether to use the mean or the median is context dependent. The mean will be more influenced by the outliers, which may be better in some scenarios, but not others.

statement: When deciding between multiple possible versions of an explanatory figure, you should always choose the one that conveys more information (i.e., is more detailed).
label: False
explanations: The amount of detail that you should present depends on your audience. A research paper may call for more details than a presentation slide or a general public-facing information pamphlet.

statement: If one variable is correlated with another, then changes in one will cause changes in the other.
label: False
explanations: Correlated variables will not necessarily be causally related. There may be another variable that simultaneously and independently affects both variables.

statement: You should evaluate the predictability and stability of every explanatory finding that you present.
label: True
explanations: You should always evaluate the predictability and stability of every explanatory finding, especially if you are going to present the findings. It is also a good idea to evaluate the predictability and stability of any exploratory findings that seem important.

statement: Not every exploratory finding needs to be turned into an explanatory figure.
label: True
explanations: You will tend to make a lot of exploratory findings, but only those that are actually conveying important information that you want to communicate to an external audience need to be turned into explanatory figures.

statement: Exploratory and explanatory data analyses can be numeric summaries (i.e., are not only data visualizations).
label: True
explanations: Exploratory (and explanatory) findings can include numeric summaries and tables.

statement: Correlation only quantifies the linear component of the relationship between two variables.
label: True
explanations: Correlation captures the strength only of the linear relationship between two variables.

statement: If one variable causes changes in the other, then the two variables will be correlated.
label: True
explanations: Variables with a causal relationship will also be correlated (but not necessarily the other way around).

statement: The technique of SVD is used only for principal component analysis.
label: False
explanations: SVD is a general technique used for a range of problems, one of which is principal component analysis.

statement: The principal component variable loading magnitudes are comparable only if the variables are mean-centered.
label: False
explanations: The principal component variable loading magnitudes are comparable only if the variables have the same scale (e.g., they have been SD-scaled).

statement: If principal component analysis is applied to data with positive values, the variable loadings will all be positive too.
label: False
explanations: Even if all the values in the data are positive, principal component analysis can still yield negative variable loadings. This is evident from the examples shown in this chapter.

statement: We are only ever interested in the first principal component.
label: False
explanations: While the first principal component typically contains the most information, there are many applications where you will want to consider multiple principal components beyond just the first one.

statement: The projected data points will exhibit greater variability when projected onto the second principal component than the first principal component.
label: False
explanations: The reverse is true: the projected data points will exhibit greater variability when projected onto the first principal component than the second principal component.

statement: The principal component analysis algorithm requires that the columns in your data have a Gaussian distribution.
label: False
explanations: Principal component analysis does not require that the original variables have a Gaussian distribution, but you will often find more meaningful components when they do.

statement: Any matrix can be decomposed using SVD.
label: True
explanations: The fact that every matrix has a SVD decomposition is what makes it such a versatile technique.

statement: Data cleaning/preprocessing judgment calls can affect the results of principal component analysis.
label: True
explanations: If you clean or preprocess your data differently, you may end up with slightly different principal components.

statement: Principal component analysis can be applied only to datasets with numeric variables.
label: True
explanations: Principal component analysis can be applied only to datasets with numeric variables. If your data contains non-numeric variables, you can still apply principal component analysis if you convert the non-numeric variables to a numeric format.

statement: Principal component analysis only creates summary variables consisting of linear combinations of the original variables.
label: True
explanations: Principal component analysis is specifically designed to compute linear summaries.

statement: A scree plot displays the proportion of variability explained by each principal component.
label: True
explanations: This is exactly what a scree plot does.

statement: Clusters are always computed using the Euclidean distance metric.
label: False
explanations: Clustering can be based on a range of different distance metrics, but the Euclidean distance metric is the most common.

statement: The K-means algorithm always converges to the minimizer of the K-means objective function.
label: False
explanations: The K-means algorithm only approximately minimizes the K-means loss function.

statement: The K-means clusters are always better than the hierarchical clusters in terms of average silhouette score.
label: False
explanations: Sometimes the K-means clusters will yield a higher silhouette score, but not always.

statement: The Rand Index can be used to compare two sets of clusters only when each set contains the same number of clusters.
label: False
explanations: The Rand Index does not require that the two sets of clusters being compared contain the same number of clusters apiece, but rather that they are based on the same sets of observations.

statement: The WSS can be used to compare two sets of clusters that each consist of different numbers of clusters.
label: False
explanations: Since the WSS will generally decrease as the number of clusters increases, it is not recommended for use when comparing sets of clusters that contain differing numbers of clusters (i.e., different values of K).

statement: Cross-validation provides a reasonable approximation to the performance of an algorithm on external data.
label: False
explanations: Since it is still based on the training data, CV does not provide a reasonable approximation of the performance of an algorithm on external data (but it is a useful technique for hyperparameter selection).

statement: The K-means algorithm is a randomized algorithm that may yield a different set of clusters every time it is run.
label: True
explanations: Since the initial cluster positions are random, the K-means clustering results may be different each time the algorithm is run.

statement: One way to define a "good" cluster is by quantifying the tightness and distinctness of the cluster.
label: True
explanations: One definition of a good cluster is indeed one that is tight and distinct.

statement: It is possible to compute the cluster centers of clusters generated from the hierarchical clustering algorithm (even though the hierarchical clustering algorithm does not itself involve computing cluster centers).
label: True
explanations: Even though the hierarchical clustering algorithm does not involve computing cluster centers, it is possible to compute the cluster centers of hierarchical clusters by computing the average value of each variable across all the observations in the cluster.

statement: The Rand Index can be used to compare two sets of clusters only for the same set of data points.
label: True
explanations: Since the Rand Index involves comparing the clustering of each pair of data points, it requires that the two sets of clusters are of the same set of data points.

statement: The silhouette score can be used to compare two sets of clusters that each consist of different numbers of clusters.
label: True
explanations: The silhouette score, unlike the WSS, can be used to compare sets of clusters that contain differing numbers of clusters (i.e., different values of K).

statement: Cross-validation is used widely in data science for conducting hyperparameter selection (i.e., it is not solely used for clustering problems).
label: True
explanations: Cross-validation (CV) is a widely used hyperparameter selection technique for a range of data science algorithms that goes beyond just clustering.

statement: Labeled data is required for training a predictive algorithm, but not for evaluating it.
label: False
explanations: Labeled data is required for both training and evaluation. If you don't know the true/observed response for the observations that you are using for evaluation, you cannot determine how accurate your predicted responses are.

statement: Creating training, validation, and test datasets using a random split will always be appropriate, no matter the domain problem or future data scenario.
label: False
explanations: There are many scenarios where a random split may not be appropriate, such as when there is a time dependence in your data or when there are repeated observations from the same person/country/group.

statement: Cluster membership labels can be thought of as real-world "ground truth" response labels for predictive problems.
label: False
explanations: Cluster labels do not necessarily correspond to real-world groups; rather, they capture groups of similar data points.

statement: Collecting more training data observations will always lead to algorithms that produce more accurate predictions.
label: False
explanations: While collecting more training data will often lead to improved predictive performance, this is not always the case.

statement: Collecting additional predictor variables will always lead to more accurate predictions.
label: False
explanations: Collecting additional predictor variables will improve the predictive performance only if the new variables have information that is actually predictive of the response variable.

statement: For any given domain problem, there are many ways that you could define a response variable.
label: True
explanations: There are often many ways to define a response variable (e.g., some response variables can be formatted as either a binary variable or a continuous variable).

statement: A predictor variable that has a strong predictive relationship with the response variable does not necessarily imply a causal relationship between the predictor and response.
label: True
explanations: A predictive relationship does not imply a causal relationship. It may be that your predictor variable tends to have large values whenever your response variable does, but this doesn't mean that an increase in the predictor variable will cause an increase in the response variable.

statement: Predictor variable, predictive feature, predictor, and covariate are all different terms used to refer to the same thing (i.e., the variables that are used to generate a prediction of a response).
label: True
explanations: These are all different terms commonly used (both in this book and outside of it) to mean the same thing.

statement: For any given set of training data points, there is an explicit mathematical formula that we can use to compute the parameters of the LAD line (i.e., the line that will minimize the absolute value loss function).
label: False
explanations: Since the absolute loss function is not differentiable at its minimum, there is no explicit mathematical formula for computing the linear fit that minimizes it.

statement: The loss function that you used to train your predictive algorithm must match the loss function that you use to evaluate the predictions.
label: False
explanations: You may use different loss functions for the processes of evaluation and training.

statement: The LAD algorithm will always produce more accurate predictions on the validation set than the LS algorithm when using the MAE predictive performance measure.
label: False
explanations: While the LAD algorithm will usually produce more accurate predictions on the validation set than the LS algorithm when using the MAE predictive performance measure, this will not always be the case.

statement: One example of a PCS predictability assessment of a predictive algorithm is to compute the MAE for the predictions computed for the training data.
label: False
explanations: One example of a predictability assessment of a predictive algorithm is to compute the MAE for the predictions computed for the validation data (rather than the training data).

statement: For any given set of training data points, there is an explicit mathematical formula that we can use to compute the parameters of the LS line (i.e., the line that will minimize the squared loss function).
label: True
explanations: Since the squared loss function is differentiable at its minimum, there is a computable formula that identifies the linear fit that minimizes it.

statement: The rMSE is on the same scale as the MAE.
label: True
explanations: Since the rMSE corresponds to the square root of the squared error, the rMSE and the MAE are on the same scale.

statement: If you have trained two predictive algorithms, it is possible for one to perform better according to the validation dataset MSE and the other to perform better according to the validation dataset MAE.
label: True
explanations: Since MSE and MAE are measuring different things, one algorithm may yield predictions that are closer to the "true" response in terms of average squared error (MSE) but not in absolute error (MAE).

statement: It is acceptable to use a predictive algorithm to predict the response of future data points that are quite different from the training data if you have shown that the algorithm generates accurate predictions for data points similar to the future data points.
label: True
explanations: If you have shown that the algorithm generates accurate predictions of data in a new context, then it is acceptable to use the algorithm in this new context.

statement: The prediction error computed on the training data does not provide an appropriate assessment of how the algorithm will perform on future data.
label: True
explanations: Since the algorithm was trained on the patterns and relationships that exist within the training data itself, being able to generate accurate predictions for the training data is no guarantee that it will be able to do so on new data (because the new data might feature slightly different patterns and relationships).

statement: The magnitude of the LS coefficient of a predictive feature corresponds to how important the feature is for generating the prediction.
label: False
explanations: This is true only if either (a) the original variables were on the same scale or have been standardized to a common scale before fitting the LS algorithm, or (b) the coefficients have been standardized (e.g., using the bootstrap) before making the comparison.

statement: Increasing the number of predictive features in a predictive fit will always improve the predictive performance.
label: False
explanations: Collecting additional predictor variables will improve the predictive performance only if the new variables contain information that is actually predictive of the response variable.

statement: The LS algorithm can only be used to train linear relationships between a response and predictor variable.
label: False
explanations: While the LS algorithm only captures linear relationships between the variables that are provided, if you apply a non-linear transformation (such as a logarithmic transformation) to either the predictor or response variables, LS can be used to capture non-linear relationships between the predictor and response variables.

statement: The best ridge and lasso regularization hyperparameter is the value that yields the smallest CV error.
label: False
explanations: It depends on how you define the "best" regularization hyperparameter. For instance, sometimes it is "better" to choose a slightly larger value of the regularization hyperparameter (e.g., the largest value within 1 SE of the value that achieves the minimum CV error).

statement: More regularization means that regularized coefficients will be closer to the original un-regularized LS coefficients.
label: False
explanations: More regularization means that the coefficients are shrunk closer to 0 (away from the original LS coefficient values).

statement: It makes more sense to use L2 (ridge) regularization than L1 (lasso) regularization for the LS algorithm because the LS algorithm involves minimizing an L2 (squared) loss function.
label: False
explanations: Although the LS algorithm involves minimizing an L2 (squared) loss function, this doesn't necessarily mean that L2 (ridge) regularization makes more sense than L1 (lasso) regularization.

statement: The LS algorithm cannot be applied directly to data with categorical predictor variables without modifying the data.
label: True
explanations: The LS algorithm requires that all the predictor variables are numeric (binary variables are a type of numeric variable). Categorical variables thus need to be transformed to a numeric type (e.g., by creating one-hot encoded/dummy variables). Many algorithmic implementations, such as lm() in R, will do this conversion under the hood for you.

statement: Correlation feature selection can be used for data that has binary predictor variables.
label: True
explanations: Although correlation isn't a particularly good measure of association for binary variables, this doesn't mean that you can't use it.

statement: The preprocessing judgment calls that you make can affect your predictive performance.
label: True
explanations: While the preprocessing stage may seem fairly removed from the prediction stage of the DSLC, the judgment calls that you make during preprocessing can absolutely affect your predictions (which is why we assess their effect on our results using stability assessments).

statement: Overfitting to the training data happens when your predictive fit captures very specific patterns that exist only in the training data and do not generalize to other similar data.
label: True
explanations: This is the very definition of overfitting.

statement: The unthresholded predictions computed by the LS algorithm for a binary response correspond to the predicted probability of being in the positive class.
label: False
explanations: Unlike the logistic regression predictions, the LS predictions for binary responses should not be interpreted as class probability predictions.

statement: The logistic regression loss can be minimized using LS and has a unique "closed form" solution.
label: False
explanations: Unfortunately, there is no closed-form solution to the logistic regression optimization problem. Moreover, it cannot be directly solved using LS because we don't ever observe the true class probabilities.

statement: We cannot conduct a stability analysis for binary prediction problems because the response variable has only two values.
label: False
explanations: There are many stability analyses that we could conduct, including investigating whether the predictive performance changes across data and cleaning/preprocessing judgment call perturbations.

statement: In medicine, it is always more important to have a high true positive rate (sensitivity) than it is to have a high true negative rate (specificity).
label: False
explanations: Whether a high true positive rate (sensitivity) is more or less important than a high true negative rate (specificity) will depend on the particular problem.

statement: For a binary predictive algorithm that always predicts the positive class, the accuracy of the algorithm evaluated on the validation set will be equal to the proportion of training data points in the positive class.
label: False
explanations: In such a case, the accuracy of this algorithm evaluated on the validation set will be equal to the proportion of validation (not training) data points in the positive class.

statement: If algorithm A has a higher AUC than algorithm B, then algorithm A will achieve better prediction accuracy than algorithm B for every choice of probability threshold value.
label: False
explanations: Even if the AUC for algorithm A is higher, there may still be individual threshold choices for which algorithm B performs better than algorithm A.

statement: The logistic regression algorithm requires that the predictive features have a Gaussian distribution.
label: False
explanations: Gaussianity of the predictive features is not a requirement for the logistic regression algorithm; however, transformations that improve the symmetry and/or Gaussianity of a feature's distribution may lead to better predictive performance.

statement: Although the LS algorithm is designed for continuous response prediction problems, it can also be used for binary response prediction problems.
label: True
explanations: We demonstrated in this chapter that LS can technically be used for binary prediction problems.

statement: Many continuous response problems can be translated into binary response problems.
label: True
explanations: One way to do this is to use a threshold value to convert a continuous response into a binary response.

statement: The logistic transformation can be used to transform a linear combination of predictive features into a predicted positive class probability.
label: True
explanations: The logistic function can indeed be used to transform a linear combination into a predicted positive class probability.

statement: Creating binary predictions using a probability prediction threshold value equal to the proportion of observations in the positive class is often a better choice than a threshold value of 0.5.
label: True
explanations: This is particularly true for prediction problems with class imbalance.

statement: The CART algorithm can only be used to construct decision trees for predicting binary responses.
label: False
explanations: CART can be used to construct decision trees for predicting binary and continuous responses.

statement: The CART algorithm is always more stable to both data perturbations and cleaning/preprocessing judgment calls than the LS algorithm.
label: False
explanations: In this chapter, we saw that the CART algorithm is substantially less stable to data perturbations relative to LS.

statement: The Gini impurity measure can be used to evaluate the validation set predictive performance of the CART algorithm.
label: False
explanations: The Gini impurity is used to train the CART algorithm using the training set, not to evaluate it using the validation set.

statement: The CART algorithm is a random algorithm (meaning that it will result in a different fit every time you train it on the same data set).
label: False
explanations: Because the CART algorithm does not involve any random sampling of observations or predictive features when computing the splits, CART is not a random algorithm (it will produce the same fit every time it is trained on the same dataset).

statement: The Gini feature importance measure can only be used to compare the importance of predictive features that have been standardized.
label: False
explanations: The RF feature importance measures do not require that you standardize the features.

statement: You can compute predictions from a reasonably small decision tree without using a computer.
label: True
explanations: This is one of the biggest benefits of the decision tree.

statement: Even though the default CART hyperparameters typically lead to fairly good predictive performance, the predictive performance can often still be improved by tuning the hyperparameters.
label: True
explanations: It is certainly possible to improve predictive performance by tuning the hyperparameters, although, in our experience, this performance improvement is usually minor.

statement: The RF algorithm is a random algorithm (meaning that it will result in a different fit every time you train it on the same data set).
label: True
explanations: The RF algorithm is random because each tree is trained using a random sample of observations, and each split considers a random subset of predictive features.

statement: The permutation importance measure is a general technique that can be used for algorithms other than the RF algorithm.
label: True
explanations: Since the permutation feature importance measure involves identifying how the predictive performance changes when you permute each feature separately (this idea is not specific to the RF algorithm), it could be used to compute a feature importance score for any predictive algorithm.

statement: Applying a log-transformation to a predictive feature does not affect the prediction output of the CART algorithm.
label: True
explanations: While log-transforming predictive features can change the individual split threshold values, it will not affect the prediction output of the CART algorithm.

statement: In the PCS framework, the final predictive fit is chosen from among several algorithms, each trained on just one cleaned and preprocessed version of the training data.
label: False
explanations: This is the traditional approach. In the PCS framework, we instead recommend considering several versions of each algorithm trained on different versions of the cleaned/preprocessed data.

statement: The members of an ensemble algorithm must all be of the same type (e.g., they should all be LS algorithms).
label: False
explanations: An ensemble can be created using a range of different algorithms, so long as they are all designed to predict the same response.

statement: The predictive performance of an ensemble will always be better than the single best predictive fit.
label: False
explanations: As we have seen in this chapter, it is certainly possible to create an ensemble fit that performs worse than the single predictive fit with the highest validation set performance.

statement: By removing the largest and smallest 5 percent of predictions when creating PPIs (i.e., basing our intervals on the 5th and 95th prediction quantiles), we force the coverage of the intervals on the validation set to be equal to 90 percent.
label: False
explanations: The uncalibrated validation set coverage will rarely be 90 percent (unless we capture all possible sources of uncertainty in our perturbations—which is essentially impossible). Calibration is required to achieve a coverage closer to our goal of 90 percent.

statement: Having trained your final predictive fit in R or Python, anyone will be able to use your fit to generate predictions if they have access to your code, regardless of their technical skill level.
label: False
explanations: Unfortunately, for many projects, the intended users of your final fit will not have the technical skills required to make use of your fit if it can only be accessed with R or Python.

statement: The output of an ensemble algorithm provides just one prediction for each data point.
label: True
explanations: An ensemble combines multiple predictions for each data point into a single prediction output.

statement: The same performance measures (e.g., correlation and rMSE for continuous response problems and accuracy, sensitivity, and AUC for binary response problems) can be used to evaluate and compare ensemble predictions and predictions from a single fit.
label: True
explanations: Since both the single prediction and ensemble predictions involve reporting a single response prediction for each data point, they can both be evaluated and compared using the standard performance measures. This is not true of the PPIs, however.

statement: After using the test set to evaluate the "final" fit, it is not a good idea to make further modifications to our fits in order to improve the test set performance.
label: True
explanations: Repeatedly using the test set to decide the final prediction (e.g., by comparing different options) means that the test set is no longer independent of the final predictions, and thus cannot be used to provide an independent assessment of predictive performance.

statement: If the top fits (in terms of the validation set predictive performance) include various alternative options for a particular cleaning/preprocessing judgment call, then the predictive performance is considered to be fairly stable (i.e., not sensitive) to this judgment call.
label: True
explanations: If various alternative options for a particular judgment call all lead to similar predictive performance, then this judgment call clearly doesn't have much influence on the predictive performance.

statement: It is important to conduct predictability screening before creating PCS ensembles and PPIs.
label: True
explanations: Since we don't want to include fits with poor performance in our ensemble or intervals, it is important to conduct predictability screening.

statement: A larger dataset is a more faithful representation of reality than a smaller one.
label: False
explanations: A large dataset collected through a biased mechanism can be less faithful to reality than a small, well-collected one.

statement: Data science conclusions become objective once the analysis is fully automated.
label: False
explanations: Automation hides judgment calls rather than removing them; the choices are still embedded in the code.

statement: Even data collected with a carefully designed instrument will always contain some measurement error.
label: True
explanations: All measurement processes are imperfect; the goal is to understand the error, not to eliminate it.

statement: Two analysts given the same dataset and the same domain question may reasonably arrive at different conclusions.
label: True
explanations: Different defensible judgment calls can lead to different results, which is why stability analysis matters.

statement: Domain knowledge is needed to judge whether a data-driven finding is meaningful in the real world.
label: True
explanations: Numerical patterns cannot be interpreted without knowledge of the data generating process and domain context.

statement: The way in which data was collected affects which questions the data can credibly answer.
label: True
explanations: The data collection mechanism determines the population and conditions the data actually represents.

statement: Your prior beliefs can influence which patterns you notice.
label: True
explanations: Confirmation bias operates during exploration, not only at the conclusion stage.

statement: Two datasets that were collected using different mechanisms may support different conclusions, even if they were intended to measure the same underlying quantity.
label: True
explanations: The collection mechanism shapes what the data represents.

statement: The measurements in a dataset are approximations of the underlying real-world quantities that they are intended to capture.
label: True
explanations: All measurement involves some degree of approximation.

statement: It is possible for a finding to be both reproducible (i.e., someone else running your code on your data obtains exactly the same numbers) and misleading about the real-world phenomenon that you set out to study.
label: True
explanations: Reproducibility concerns consistency of computation, not correctness of interpretation.

statement: A dataset that contains millions of observations is a more faithful representation of reality than one that contains hundreds.
label: False
explanations: A large dataset collected through a biased mechanism can be less faithful than a small, carefully collected one.

statement: Once your analysis has been automated, the conclusions that it produces are objective (i.e., they no longer depend on your judgment calls).
label: False
explanations: Automation embeds the judgment calls in code rather than removing them.

statement: The values recorded in a dataset can be treated as exact measurements of reality if the data was collected by a machine rather than by a human.
label: False
explanations: Instruments have their own measurement error and calibration issues.

statement: If you did not personally collect the data, then you do not need to understand how it was collected.
label: False
explanations: Understanding the collection process is necessary regardless of who carried it out.

statement: The computability principle in PCS refers to how easily a domain expert can understand the results.
label: False
explanations: That is a matter of communication; computability concerns computational feasibility and efficiency.

statement: A thorough stability analysis removes the need for domain knowledge.
label: False
explanations: Stability tells you whether a result persists across choices, not whether it is meaningful in the domain.

statement: Stability analyses can involve perturbing the data, the cleaning judgment calls, or the algorithm itself.
label: True
explanations: Stability is assessed across the full range of choices made during an analysis, not only across data perturbations.

statement: The computability principle includes consideration of the memory and runtime that an analysis requires.
label: True
explanations: Computability concerns whether an analysis can actually be carried out with available computational resources.

statement: The predictability principle involves checking whether a result reemerges in data that was not used to produce it.
label: True
explanations: Predictability asks whether a finding holds up on new or held-out data.

statement: You can evaluate the stability of a result by perturbing the data, by making alternative cleaning judgment calls, or by using a different algorithm.
label: True
explanations: Stability is assessed across the full range of defensible analytic choices.

statement: The computability principle involves considering whether an analysis can actually be carried out using the computational resources that you have available.
label: True
explanations: Computability concerns feasibility, memory, and runtime.

statement: A PCS evaluation can reveal that a finding you were confident about is not stable, in which case you should report the instability rather than presenting the finding as though it were settled.
label: True
explanations: That is much of the point of conducting one.

statement: It is possible for a result to be stable but not predictable.
label: True
explanations: A result can reappear across perturbations of the same data and still fail on held-out data.

statement: The computability principle in the PCS framework refers to how easily your results can be understood by a domain expert who has no programming experience.
label: False
explanations: That is a communication issue; computability concerns computational feasibility.

statement: A thorough stability analysis removes the need to consult domain experts about whether your findings make sense.
label: False
explanations: Stability shows that a result persists, not that it is meaningful.

statement: The predictability principle is satisfied as long as your algorithm achieves low error on the data that you used to train it.
label: False
explanations: Predictability requires evaluation on data that was not used to produce the result.

statement: You should conduct your PCS evaluations only after you have finished every other stage of the DSLC.
label: False
explanations: PCS evaluations are conducted throughout the life cycle.

statement: Reproducibility guarantees that a finding will generalize to a new population.
label: False
explanations: Reproducing the same computation says nothing about whether the finding transfers to different data.

statement: Saving the cleaned data file instead of the cleaning code is sufficient for a reproducible workflow.
label: False
explanations: Without the code, the judgment calls that produced the cleaned file cannot be inspected or rerun.

statement: Setting a random seed is necessary for making the output of a randomized algorithm reproducible.
label: True
explanations: Without a fixed seed, a randomized algorithm produces different output on each run.

statement: Two researchers can obtain identical numerical results from the same data and code while both being wrong.
label: True
explanations: Reproducibility in this sense certifies consistency of computation, not correctness of the conclusion.

statement: Recording the version of each software package used improves the reproducibility of an analysis.
label: True
explanations: Results can change across package versions, so versions are part of the computational environment.

statement: Setting a random seed is necessary if you want a randomized algorithm to produce the same output every time it is run.
label: True
explanations: Without a fixed seed the output differs across runs.

statement: Recording your software package versions aids reproducibility.
label: True
explanations: Results can change across package versions.

statement: Two people can obtain identical numerical results from the same data and code while both being wrong.
label: True
explanations: Computational reproducibility does not certify correctness.

statement: If your results are reproducible, then they will also hold in a new population.
label: False
explanations: Reproducing a computation says nothing about transfer to different data.

statement: Saving your cleaned data file is sufficient documentation of your cleaning process (i.e., you do not also need to save the code that produced it).
label: False
explanations: Without the code the judgment calls cannot be inspected or rerun.

statement: Comments in your code are unnecessary as long as your variable names are descriptive.
label: False
explanations: Names describe what a value is, not why a choice was made.

statement: A tidy project folder guarantees a correct analysis.
label: False
explanations: Organization aids reproducibility but says nothing about correctness.

statement: Discarding an observation with an implausible value is preferable to investigating why the value is implausible.
label: False
explanations: Implausible values often reveal something important about how the data was collected or recorded.

statement: Preprocessing decisions should be finalized by comparing test set performance across the options.
label: False
explanations: Using the test set to make preprocessing choices contaminates it and invalidates the final evaluation.

statement: Whether a missing value should be imputed depends on the reason the value is missing.
label: True
explanations: The appropriate treatment differs depending on the mechanism that generated the missingness.

statement: Converting a variable stored as text into a numeric format is an example of a data cleaning action.
label: True
explanations: Correcting the format of a variable so that it can be analyzed is part of cleaning.

statement: Imputing missing values with the mean of a variable reduces the sample variance of that variable.
label: True
explanations: The imputed values sit exactly at the mean and add nothing to the sum of squared deviations, while increasing the number of observations.

statement: How you should handle a missing value depends on why you think the value is missing.
label: True
explanations: The appropriate treatment depends on the missingness mechanism.

statement: Converting a variable that was stored as text into a numeric format is an example of a data cleaning action.
label: True
explanations: Correcting a variable's format so that it can be analyzed is part of cleaning.

statement: Two people cleaning the same dataset may produce two different clean datasets, and both may be defensible.
label: True
explanations: Cleaning involves judgment calls with no single correct answer.

statement: Invalid values often tell you something about data collection.
label: True
explanations: Implausible values frequently reveal recording or instrument problems.

statement: The most efficient approach to an implausible value is to remove the observation rather than investigate why the value is implausible.
label: False
explanations: Investigating implausible values often reveals important information about the data.

statement: You should choose among alternative preprocessing options by comparing their performance on the test set.
label: False
explanations: Using the test set for選 selection contaminates it and invalidates the final evaluation.

statement: Variables with no missing values need no cleaning.
label: False
explanations: Complete variables can still contain invalid, mis-scaled, or mis-typed values.

statement: If two different cleaning judgment calls lead to the same conclusion, then that conclusion must be correct.
label: False
explanations: Agreement across choices is evidence of stability, not of correctness.

statement: A correlation of zero between two variables indicates that they are independent.
label: False
explanations: Zero correlation rules out a linear relationship only; the variables can still be strongly dependent.

statement: Pie charts convey proportions more accurately than bar charts.
label: False
explanations: People compare lengths more accurately than angles or areas, so bar charts are generally clearer.

statement: A variable can have a strong nonlinear relationship with another variable and still have a correlation near zero.
label: True
explanations: Correlation measures only the linear component of a relationship.

statement: The median is unchanged when the largest value in a dataset is increased further.
label: True
explanations: The median depends on the ordering of values, not on the magnitude of the extremes.

statement: The appearance of a histogram can change substantially depending on the bin width that is chosen.
label: True
explanations: Bin width is a judgment call that affects the visual impression of the distribution.

statement: Applying a log transformation to a right-skewed variable before plotting can make patterns easier to see.
label: True
explanations: The transformation spreads out the compressed low values and pulls in the long tail.

statement: An explanatory figure must always be interpretable without the analyst present to explain it.
label: True
explanations: Explanatory figures are intended to communicate a finding to an audience on their own.

statement: Changing the bin width of a histogram can substantially change the impression that it gives of the distribution.
label: True
explanations: Bin width is a judgment call with visual consequences.

statement: Two plots of the same data can suggest different conclusions.
label: True
explanations: Visualization choices shape interpretation.

statement: You should check whether an exploratory finding is stable before you turn it into an explanatory figure.
label: True
explanations: Only findings that survive PCS evaluation are worth presenting.

statement: A summary statistic can be a perfectly accurate description of your data and still be misleading about the world.
label: True
explanations: Accuracy with respect to the data does not imply accuracy with respect to reality.

statement: Every exploratory figure that you create should eventually be polished into an explanatory figure.
label: False
explanations: Most exploratory figures are for you alone and are never presented.

statement: The variability of a numeric variable is best summarized using its range, since the range is the only summary that reflects every possible value that the variable takes in your dataset.
label: False
explanations: The range depends on only two observations and is highly sensitive to outliers.

statement: A scatterplot is always the best way to display the relationship between two numeric variables.
label: False
explanations: With very many points or heavy overplotting, other displays communicate better.

statement: You should include as many variables as possible in a single figure so that the reader has complete information.
label: False
explanations: Overloaded figures obscure the finding that they are meant to convey.

statement: The first principal component is the line passing through the two most distant data points.
label: False
explanations: The first component is the direction of greatest variance across all points, not a line through two of them.

statement: Principal components with small explained variance can be discarded without affecting any downstream analysis.
label: False
explanations: A low-variance direction can still carry information that matters for a particular downstream task.

statement: The loadings of a principal component sum to one.
label: False
explanations: The loadings form a unit vector, so it is the sum of their squares that equals one.

statement: The principal components are always orthogonal to one another.
label: True
explanations: Each successive component is constructed to be orthogonal to all previous ones.

statement: Standardizing the variables before conducting principal component analysis is recommended when the variables are measured on different scales.
label: True
explanations: Without standardization, variables with larger numeric scales dominate the components.

statement: The number of principal components that can be computed is at most the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns.
label: True
explanations: The rank of the data matrix bounds the number of nonzero components.

statement: Reversing the signs of a principal component's loadings and scores gives an equally valid representation.
label: True
explanations: The direction of a component is determined only up to sign.

statement: You can apply principal component analysis to a dataset that has more columns than rows.
label: True
explanations: The algorithm runs; the number of nonzero components is bounded by the smaller dimension.

statement: The first principal component is the direction along which the projected data points exhibit the greatest variability.
label: True
explanations: This is the defining property of the first component.

statement: You can assess PCA stability by perturbing the data.
label: True
explanations: Data perturbation is one of the standard PCS stability checks.

statement: The proportion of variability explained by each successive principal component is non-increasing.
label: True
explanations: Components are ordered by decreasing explained variance, which is why scree plots decline.

statement: The scores of the first principal component are always positively correlated with every original variable.
label: False
explanations: Loadings can be negative, so scores can be negatively correlated with some variables.

statement: If you apply principal component analysis twice to the same data, you will obtain different components each time (i.e., it is a randomized algorithm).
label: False
explanations: The computation is deterministic up to the sign of each component.

statement: PCA selects a subset of your original variables.
label: False
explanations: It creates new linear combinations rather than selecting among the original variables.

statement: The variable loadings of the first principal component tell you which variables are causally important.
label: False
explanations: Loadings describe covariation in the data and carry no causal information.

statement: Hierarchical clustering requires the number of clusters to be chosen before the algorithm is run.
label: False
explanations: The number of clusters is chosen afterward by cutting the dendrogram.

statement: A high average silhouette score confirms that the clusters correspond to real subpopulations.
label: False
explanations: Silhouette measures geometric separation in the data; it cannot establish real-world meaning.

statement: Increasing the number of clusters in K-means reduces the within-cluster sum of squares only when the additional clusters are meaningful.
label: False
explanations: The within-cluster sum of squares decreases as K increases regardless of whether the clusters are meaningful.

statement: The number of clusters must be specified in advance for the K-means algorithm.
label: True
explanations: K is an input to the algorithm and is not determined by it.

statement: A dendrogram can be cut at different heights to produce different numbers of clusters.
label: True
explanations: Hierarchical clustering produces a nested sequence of groupings rather than a single partition.

statement: Standardizing the variables before clustering can change which observations end up grouped together.
label: True
explanations: Distance calculations depend on the scale of each variable.

statement: The silhouette score of an individual observation can be negative.
label: True
explanations: A negative value indicates the observation is closer on average to a neighboring cluster than to its own.

statement: You must specify the number of clusters in advance when you apply the K-means algorithm.
label: True
explanations: K is an input to the algorithm.

statement: Standardizing your variables before clustering can change which observations end up in the same cluster.
label: True
explanations: Distance calculations depend on the scale of each variable.

statement: The silhouette score of an individual data point can be negative, which indicates that the point is closer on average to the members of a neighboring cluster than it is to the members of its own cluster.
label: True
explanations: A negative value means the point is closer on average to a neighboring cluster than to its own.

statement: Two different linkage choices in hierarchical clustering can produce very different sets of clusters from the same data.
label: True
explanations: Linkage is a judgment call that materially affects the result.

statement: The number of clusters must be specified before the hierarchical clustering algorithm is run.
label: False
explanations: The number is chosen afterward by cutting the dendrogram.

statement: A high average silhouette score confirms that your clusters correspond to real subpopulations in the world.
label: False
explanations: Silhouette measures geometric separation, not real-world meaning.

statement: The clusters produced by the K-means algorithm will be the same regardless of the units in which your variables are measured.
label: False
explanations: Changing units changes distances and therefore changes the clusters.

statement: If two different clustering algorithms produce similar clusters, then the clusters must reflect real structure.
label: False
explanations: Two algorithms can share the same assumptions and be similarly misled.

statement: The validation set provides an unbiased estimate of how the final chosen fit will perform on future data.
label: False
explanations: Because the validation set is used to choose among fits, its error is optimistically biased for the winner.

statement: A predictor variable with a small correlation with the response can be safely excluded from consideration.
label: False
explanations: A variable with weak marginal correlation can still be useful in combination with others.

statement: A response variable that is expensive to measure may still be worth predicting from cheaper predictor variables.
label: True
explanations: Replacing an expensive measurement with a prediction is a common motivation for a predictive project.

statement: When data points are collected over time, splitting by time rather than at random can better mimic the future data scenario.
label: True
explanations: A time-based split reflects the reality that future data comes after the training data.

statement: The test set should always be reserved for a single evaluation at the end of the project.
label: True
explanations: Repeated use of the test set turns it into a selection set and inflates the reported performance.

statement: How you define your response variable is itself a judgment call that can change your conclusions.
label: True
explanations: There are usually several defensible ways to define a response.

statement: It is possible to have a well-posed predictive problem for which none of the predictor variables that were actually collected carry useful information about the response, in which case no algorithm will produce accurate predictions.
label: True
explanations: Data availability constrains what can be predicted.

statement: You can evaluate a predictive algorithm only if you have access to the true response values for the data points that you are evaluating it on.
label: True
explanations: Evaluation requires ground truth labels.

statement: You should decide on your future data scenario before you split your data into training, validation, and test sets.
label: True
explanations: The intended future scenario determines which splitting strategy is appropriate.

statement: If your training and test sets are drawn from the same data, then your test set performance will reflect your performance on future data.
label: False
explanations: Future data may differ systematically from the data you currently have.

statement: The response variable for a predictive problem is determined by the data (i.e., you do not get to choose it).
label: False
explanations: Defining the response is a modeling choice made by the analyst.

statement: A larger validation set always leads to a better choice of final fit, because the validation performance estimates on which the choice is based become more precise as the number of validation data points increases.
label: False
explanations: A larger validation set leaves less training data and does not guarantee a better choice.

statement: If your algorithm performs well on the validation set, then it will perform well on any future data.
label: False
explanations: Validation performance is not a guarantee under distribution shift.

statement: The rMSE and the MAE will always rank two competing algorithms in the same order.
label: False
explanations: The two measures weight large errors differently and can disagree.

statement: The LS line minimizes the perpendicular distance from each data point to the line.
label: False
explanations: Least squares minimizes vertical distances in the response direction, not perpendicular distances.

statement: Between two fits, the one with lower training error is the preferable choice.
label: False
explanations: Lower training error may simply reflect overfitting; performance on held-out data is what matters.

statement: The MAE is always less than or equal to the rMSE computed on the same set of prediction errors.
label: True
explanations: Squaring places extra weight on large errors, so the root mean squared error is never smaller.

statement: Squared loss places more weight on large errors than absolute value loss does.
label: True
explanations: Squaring grows faster than the absolute value as the error increases.

statement: A predictive algorithm can have low training error and high validation error.
label: True
explanations: This pattern is the signature of overfitting.

statement: If you change the units in which the response variable is measured, the rMSE will change too.
label: True
explanations: The rMSE is on the scale of the response.

statement: It is possible for a predictive algorithm to perform well on average while performing very poorly for an identifiable subgroup of data points.
label: True
explanations: Aggregate measures can hide subgroup failures.

statement: The correlation between the predicted and the observed responses can be high even when the predictions are systematically too large.
label: True
explanations: Correlation is invariant to a shift in the predictions.

statement: You should report the predictive performance computed on the validation set rather than the performance computed on the training data.
label: True
explanations: Training error is optimistic and does not describe future performance.

statement: A predictive algorithm that achieves an rMSE of zero on the validation set has been trained correctly.
label: False
explanations: An rMSE of exactly zero usually indicates leakage between the splits.

statement: If your rMSE is small, then your predictions are accurate for every data point in the validation set.
label: False
explanations: A small average error is compatible with a few very large individual errors.

statement: The MAE and the rMSE are measured on different scales, so they cannot be directly compared.
label: False
explanations: Both are on the scale of the response variable.

statement: Ridge regularization performs feature selection by setting coefficients exactly to zero.
label: False
explanations: Ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero but does not generally set them exactly to zero.

statement: Standardizing the predictors before applying ridge regression is unnecessary.
label: False
explanations: The ridge penalty depends on coefficient magnitude, which depends on the scale of each predictor.

statement: Lasso regularization can set some coefficients exactly to zero.
label: True
explanations: The L1 penalty produces sparse solutions, which is why lasso performs feature selection.

statement: The scale on which a predictor variable is measured affects the magnitude of its LS coefficient.
label: True
explanations: Rescaling a predictor rescales its coefficient by the inverse factor.

statement: Regularization introduces bias in exchange for a reduction in variance.
label: True
explanations: Shrinking coefficients trades some bias for improved stability and often better test performance.

statement: You should standardize your predictive features before applying ridge or lasso regularization, because the penalty term depends on the magnitude of each coefficient, which in turn depends on the scale on which the corresponding feature was measured.
label: True
explanations: The penalty depends on coefficient magnitude, which depends on feature scale.

statement: A heavily regularized predictive fit may perform worse on the training data than an unregularized fit while performing better on the validation data.
label: True
explanations: That trade is the purpose of regularization.

statement: Feature selection is itself a judgment call whose effect on your results can be evaluated using a stability analysis.
label: True
explanations: Alternative feature sets are one of the perturbations PCS considers.

statement: The regularization hyperparameter should be chosen by comparing the training error across a grid of candidate values and selecting the value that produces the smallest training error.
label: False
explanations: It is selected using validation or cross-validation error.

statement: If a feature's coefficient is set to zero by the lasso algorithm, then that feature is unrelated to the response.
label: False
explanations: A feature can be dropped because a correlated feature was retained instead.

statement: Two predictive features that are highly correlated with one another will always receive similar lasso coefficients.
label: False
explanations: Lasso tends to select one of a correlated pair and shrink the other toward zero.

statement: Overfitting can be diagnosed by examining the training error alone (i.e., if the training error is very small, then you know that your predictive fit has overfit the training data).
label: False
explanations: Overfitting is visible only in the gap between training and held-out performance.

statement: A logistic regression coefficient of 0.5 means the predicted probability rises by 0.5 for a one-unit increase in the feature.
label: False
explanations: The coefficient acts on the log-odds scale, not directly on the probability scale.

statement: Specificity is the proportion of predicted positives that are truly positive.
label: False
explanations: That describes precision; specificity is the proportion of true negatives that are correctly identified.

statement: Increasing the probability threshold used to create binary predictions can never increase sensitivity.
label: True
explanations: A higher threshold produces fewer positive predictions, so the true positive rate cannot rise.

statement: The AUC is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of the predicted probabilities.
label: True
explanations: The AUC depends only on the ranking of the predictions.

statement: A classifier with an AUC of 0.5 performs no better than random guessing.
label: True
explanations: An AUC of 0.5 means the predictions carry no ranking information about the class.

statement: Accuracy can be a misleading performance measure when the classes are highly imbalanced.
label: True
explanations: Always predicting the majority class can produce high accuracy while being useless.

statement: You can compute the sensitivity and the specificity only after you have chosen a probability threshold value.
label: True
explanations: Both are defined on binary predictions, which require a threshold.

statement: Which of sensitivity and specificity matters more depends on the domain problem and on the consequences of each type of error.
label: True
explanations: The relative cost of false positives and false negatives is domain specific.

statement: It is possible for a binary predictive algorithm to have high accuracy and a sensitivity of zero.
label: True
explanations: Always predicting the negative class does exactly this when the positive class is rare.

statement: A binary predictive algorithm can be evaluated using several different performance measures that disagree with one another.
label: True
explanations: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC can rank algorithms differently.

statement: The AUC can be computed only after you have chosen a probability threshold value.
label: False
explanations: The AUC aggregates performance across all thresholds.

statement: Since the logistic regression algorithm produces probabilities, its predictions do not need to be evaluated for stability.
label: False
explanations: Producing probabilities has no bearing on whether the fit is stable across perturbations.

statement: A confusion matrix computed using a threshold of 0.5 provides a complete summary of a binary algorithm's performance.
label: False
explanations: It describes performance at one threshold only.

statement: Deeper decision trees generalize better to future data than shallower ones.
label: False
explanations: Deeper trees fit the training data more closely and often generalize worse.

statement: Two predictive features with similar Gini importance contribute equally to every individual prediction.
label: False
explanations: Gini importance is an aggregate summary and does not describe any individual prediction.

statement: A decision tree can capture interactions between predictor variables without those interactions being specified in advance.
label: True
explanations: Successive splits on different variables represent interactions implicitly.

statement: Increasing the maximum depth of a decision tree will never decrease its training set accuracy.
label: True
explanations: Additional splits can only refine the fit to the training data.

statement: The RF algorithm reduces variance by averaging predictions across many trees.
label: True
explanations: Averaging over many randomized trees stabilizes the prediction.

statement: The predictions of a decision tree are unchanged by a monotonic transformation of a single predictor variable.
label: True
explanations: Splits depend only on the ordering of the values of the predictor.

statement: The CART algorithm can be applied to data whose predictive features are measured on very different scales without standardizing them first.
label: True
explanations: Splits depend on the ordering of values within each feature.

statement: A single decision tree is generally easier to explain to a domain expert than an RF fit is.
label: True
explanations: A tree can be drawn and read directly; an ensemble of trees cannot.

statement: Each RF tree is trained on a bootstrapped sample.
label: True
explanations: Bootstrap sampling is one of the two sources of randomness in the algorithm.

statement: The CART algorithm produces a fit whose predictions can be described as a series of yes-or-no questions.
label: True
explanations: Each split is a binary condition on one feature.

statement: The RF algorithm produces a single interpretable tree.
label: False
explanations: It produces many trees whose predictions are aggregated.

statement: Since the RF algorithm averages many trees, its predictions do not need to be evaluated on a validation set.
label: False
explanations: Averaging reduces variance but does not remove the need for held-out evaluation.

statement: The CART algorithm cannot be used when some of the predictive features are categorical (i.e., you must first convert every categorical feature into a set of binary indicator variables before you can train a decision tree).
label: False
explanations: CART handles categorical features directly.

statement: Increasing the number of trees in an RF fit will eventually cause it to overfit the training data.
label: False
explanations: Adding trees stabilizes the average and does not induce overfitting in the usual sense.

statement: Averaging more fits into an ensemble reduces the need to conduct predictability screening.
label: False
explanations: Including poorly predictive fits degrades the ensemble; screening remains necessary.

statement: A 90 percent prediction interval contains 90 percent of the training data points by construction.
label: False
explanations: Coverage is a property to be evaluated on held-out data, not something guaranteed on the training set.
